A QUICK FIELD GUIDE

Small boards.
Long-term thinking.

How to play

  1. Place X or O in an empty cell on the highlighted board.
  2. The cell’s position chooses the next board: top-right cell → top-right board.
  3. Win a small board with three in a row. It closes and belongs to you.
  4. If sent to a won or full board, choose any open board.
  5. Win three small boards in a row to win the game. A full small board without a winner is neutral; if all boards close without a big line, the game is a draw.

How the bots learn

Two independent, zero-initialised linear policies learn with REINFORCE policy gradients. They see 18 engineered action features (captures, blocks, threats, positions and destination-board risk). No move is forced by these features: their weights start at zero and are learned.

Each bot receives +1 for winning, −1 for losing and 0 for a draw, plus +0.12 for claiming a small board and −0.12 when the opponent claims one. Discount is 0.99 per own decision. A moving baseline reduces update variance. Starting player alternates each game.

Exploration starts at 65% and decays to 4%. The gradient accounts for this random-choice mixture. Updates happen only after completed self-play games. Watching and acceleration use the same learner; acceleration shows sampled live positions.

What the chart tells you

Every 250 games, both policies play 40 games against a frozen random policy with fixed random seeds and balanced first turns. Exploration is disabled but learned policies still sample moves. Evaluation games do not train the bots. The tougher test uses a fixed tactical opponent over 80 games per agent.

This is a lightweight browser RL experiment, not a solved-game engine. Scores can fluctuate or regress, and self-play does not guarantee optimal play. Training runs only while this page is open; devices may throttle background tabs.

Saving

Policy weights, counts and evaluation history save on this browser every evaluation and when paused. Export a checkpoint to move devices. An unfinished game and the exact random-generator position are not restored. Human matches do not train the agents.
